title: Sam Altman doesn't like Elon Musk's vision of a future where humans are 'happy' pets to AI
excerpt: "I don't want to be a Labrador," Altman said, knocking Musk's vision that a super-intelligent AI could surpass humanity and domesticate us all.
content_html:
2026-11-18T18:22:24.386Z

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's rivalry with Elon Musk has gone to the dogs.

On Wednesday, Altman knocked Musk for previously suggesting that AI could become so powerful that it would relegate humanity to the role of a house pet.

"I don't want to be a Labrador. I don't want my kids to be Labradors," Altman said during an onstage interview at The New York Times Dealbook summit. "I want people to have the agency over the future that we have had."

In July, The Economist asked Musk about a comment he made more than a decade ago that if AI advanced too quickly, it would make humans "like a pet Labrador."

"Labradors are pretty happy creatures, that's my experience," Musk told The Economist while chuckling.

In 2015, Musk and astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson discussed what would happen if artificial intelligence reached the stage of recursive self-improvement, where AI becomes so advanced that it can begin advancing itself with minimal or no human guidance. Some in AI have said that if that stage is reached, AI will improve so rapidly that it could quickly surpass human intelligence and potentially any means of controlling the technology.

"That's all she wrote," Musk said, repeating Tyson's words.

Musk described being worried that a recursively self-improving AI "could reprogram itself to be smarter and iterate very quickly and do that 24 hours a day on millions of computers."

What Musk talked about then (almost eight years before ChatGPT's release) is less theoretical now.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Altman, and Musk all endorsed Amodei's September call to slow frontier AI research that pushes models toward self-improvement and to use the time in between to find more effective ways to ensure the models remain under human control.

Altman has repeatedly said in recent weeks that he wants to ensure the industry doesn't accept any scenario in which humans cede control to AI. He has said he is not convinced that his competitors feel the same way.

"We both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future," Altman told Dealbook on Wednesday, while being joined onstage by OpenAI President Greg Brockman. "And there's increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. And we both agree that that's a terrible idea."

While tamer than some of their back-and-forths, Altman and Musk have a long-running feud dating back to Musk's anger over OpenAI's shift in direction. Musk cofounded the AI lab and was an early financial backer. In May, a jury ruled that Musk waited too long to sue Altman and OpenAI over the matter.

At times, Musk has expressed alarm about humanity essentially being domesticated.

"I don't love the idea of being a house cat," Musk said in 2016.

Musk said then that the way to prevent such an outcome was to hook human brains into computers.
